summary: A catch-up sweep and the weekly deep pass, run after three scheduled sweeps did not complete. No confidence moved. The morning's link put cache translation between models under lever 1. The deep pass then found a provider, Sarvam, running the loop in production with a simulator in front of live tests; a simulator whose scheduling policies held on real hardware; an outside index on which all six shipped routers lost to a single model on score and cost; GitHub moving its router to every prompt; and Harvey tuning four newer open models after its August tune was passed within three months. W3 and W17 are settled. The roster check found 31 teams earlier passes had missed, 24 of them recorded second-hand; the roster now holds 62. Eight signals were retired or superseded to return to eighty active. Eight signals in one day is well over the guide of three. It reflects four days of backlog and a first deep pass, and is not a pattern to keep.

changes.text: An outside index ran six shipped routers on about 1,250 long agentic tasks. None sits on the cost and accuracy frontier; the best cost a third of its pool's top model for 3.9 points less, and one cheap open model beat all six on both. It supersedes a vendor's preliminary figure for the same router.
Hit. The Evolving Infra repository is public with instructions to deploy, benchmark and reproduce. No outside reproduction of its headline numbers yet.
Corrected the same day: code and weights for the cache translator are public, as a separate package that injects a translated cache into stock vLLM. The morning's entry said there was no code.

W2, W6, W19, W20, W22 and W25 annotated with what a research pass found on 26 Nov. The W20 note matters most: three measured sets, not yet opened first-hand, are reported to show speculation holding up with load on mixture-of-experts models, which would undo T10's lean.

A provider runs the loop in production: an orchestrator agent, a calibrated simulator, live A/B tests, an engineer's approval. First token 2.1x sooner than the stock stack on the same nodes; a shared cache store cut prefill nodes from 58 to 34; an upstream fused kernel had garbled one long code reply in nine.

Four open models post-trained on one customer's legal benchmark rose 11 to 21 points; one passed the best closed model, 30.3% against 27.1%. The customer's August tune had been passed by an untuned model within three months.
A CPU-only simulator with 6.7% median error against real runs. Two scheduling policies developed inside it held on hardware and were merged into llm-d. The first counter-evidence to C4 with a number.

GitHub's router now decides for every prompt and is reported ahead of the leading single models on a public agentic board. It supersedes the June signal, in which the same company routed only at cache boundaries.

Six signals retired, and two superseded by newer sources on the same products: a learned-latency scheduler, an agentic RL recipe, two on-device runtime posts, a routing-headroom benchmark and an evaluator language. Each was cited by at most one list and its point is made elsewhere with measurements. The two on-device ones can come back if local serving becomes its own thread.

Six second-hand sources opened first-hand: Databricks Smart Routing and its documentation, vLLM's Kimi K3 and AgentX posts, DFlash 2 with its model card, Baseten's agent-built engine and Harvey Tenet. Every number held. Corrections: the Kimi K3 gain on agent traces compares 16 GPUs with an earlier run on 8; DFlash 2's tables by load are on the model card, not in the post; Databricks' cost figure is against a frontier model, and its post names making a mid-session switch cheap as the next step.
Reopened. GitHub moved from the once-per-session side to the every-prompt side, and Databricks says switching must get cheaper. The lean toward cache boundaries no longer holds.

Leans more firmly toward a good default. An outside index ran six shipped routers on tasks it chose and each lost on score and cost to a single model. It stays open because sessions were not live, cache pricing was not stated, and one newer router, reported ahead on another board by its vendor, was not tested.
Lean sharpened: tuning works on a narrow job and has to be repeated. One customer's tune lasted under three months before general models passed it.
Hit. The August legal tune, 19.7%, was passed by an untuned general model at 27.1% within three months; re-tuning newer bases reached 30.3%.

W26 opened to read a new end-to-end benchmark of the loop in full before weighing it against C1. W27 opened to open TileRT's own pages, a closed engine said to have led one board since September. W5 and W20 annotated.
New chart under More charts: post-training open models on one customer's legal benchmark, with the best closed model as the reference line.

Levers 1, 3 and 6, build steps 2, 3, 7 and 8, and the open-ground item on judging unseen traffic updated. BLIS joined the build parts. The roster grew from 31 to 62 and its recent view now starts on 15 October; the front page's second point was recounted.

None moved. C4 held at 0.80: one condition on each side occurred in part, an upstream fused kernel that shipped a bug and a simulator whose policies held on hardware. C10 held at 0.45: a tune was overtaken within a quarter, and re-tuning passed the best closed model. C9 held at 0.65, but its parts are separating: models do share the work, cheap closed models now contest the routine slot, and routers and cache translation both work around the cache limit. Consider splitting it at the next deep pass. C7 held at 0.55 pending W5 and W27.
The provider implication on routing now says one router reports beating leading single models on a public board with an all-closed pool. No verdict changed.

One translator carries a cache between seven open models in all 42 directions, keeping 96.9% of accuracy up to 8,000 tokens, 92% at 32,000 and 83% at 128,000, with the first token 2.5 to 7.5x sooner at long contexts.
A serving system for the same idea, and the only test on agent tasks under load: first-token time 30 to 98% lower than a re-read after a 14B to 32B switch.
The cheapest version: a linear map within one family, fitted on 500 samples with no training. It kept 73 to 98% on four of six pairs and failed on two.
New chart under More charts on the Evidence tab: what a translated cache costs in accuracy, by method and context length.
A third side added. Besides choosing the model once or pricing the cache miss every turn, three research systems make the switch itself cheap. The lean stays toward cache boundaries until one ships.
Opened, due 2027-02-28: cache transfer reaching an open engine or a product, or an outside test on agent sessions with tool calls.

Lever 1 now says the tie between a cache and one model is being worked on. Open ground gained a sixth item, moving a session between models without a re-read. Base Labs and an arXiv query joined the feeds, and cache translation joined the glossary.

The reader sees routing as central, for local use too, and asked that cache transfer between models be tracked with it. Recorded in the steering list. The verdict that the parts are one move holds; its note now names this as the first attempt to cut one of the ties.

swept: Inbox empty at the start of the pass. No watchlist check was due; W17 was settled early because its answer turned up.

Feeds since 21 Nov, scanned by a sub-agent: vLLM blog and RFCs, Inferact, LMSYS through its sitemap, Together, AgentX optimisations, InferenceBench, llm-d, Baseten and its research site, PyTorch, Modular, OpenRouter, Fireworks, Doubleword, Vals, vLLM looped-model issues and four arXiv queries. The SemiAnalysis newsletter returned no posts and was not checked.

Roster check by kind of team, by a sub-agent: providers, open engines, model labs, chip vendors, workload owners, academics and the public board. Seven of the 29 additions were then opened first-hand; the other 22 are marked relayed.

Red-team of all four focus claims, by a sub-agent, with the decisive pages opened first-hand: BLIS, GitHub's two Fusion posts and OpenRouter's router board, which still shows single models ahead of its coding router on coding tasks.

X, through web search limited to x.com, by a sub-agent that also checked every open dated question. Single posts were opened without signing in. It surfaced an individual's agent-run tuning campaign, the code release for the cache translator, a foundation's claim of merged agent-written fixes, and two router comparisons; the Vals index, the two repositories and one abstract were then opened first-hand.

First-hand reads for the deep pass: Databricks Smart Routing and its docs, vLLM Kimi K3, vLLM AgentX, DFlash 2 and its model card, Baseten's agent-built engine, Harvey Tenet, Sarvam Token Factory, Databricks Proteus, Reflection Beam on vLLM, Morph, Cursor's kernel harness, and the abstracts of NoeVera, DuoDiscover, CompoundingKernel, RSIBench-Infra and BLIS.
The morning's single-topic update: the reader's link on cache translation, three of the papers it builds on, two web searches and one search limited to x.com.

Two research agents reported a banner on inferencex.semianalysis.com saying the copy was unaffiliated and might be modified. Opened in a browser, the page shows no such banner; it looks like an artefact of their fetch tool.

Text addressed to agents, ignored: a file on the public board's site says it is intended for language models; two repository readmes and one blog post carry launch prompts for coding agents; llama.cpp's contributing guide tells contributors to load a file into their agent.
